title: The troubleshooting methodology (the A+ 6-step model)
monthTitle: The Helpdesk Professional: ITIL, Ticketing & Soft Skills
summary: Learn the CompTIA A+ six-step troubleshooting model so you fix problems methodically instead of guessing, and document them as you go.
objectives: Recite the six steps of the CompTIA A+ troubleshooting methodology in order
Gather information and identify symptoms before changing anything
Form and test one theory of probable cause at a time
Verify full system functionality and apply preventive measures
Document findings, actions, and outcomes in the ticket
Apply the full method to a realistic support scenario

quiz.q: What is the correct first step of the A+ troubleshooting methodology?
quiz.why: Step one is always to identify the problem by gathering information, asking the user, and noting symptoms before touching anything.

quiz.q: After you establish a theory of probable cause, what comes next?
options: Test the theory to determine the cause
quiz.why: Step three is to test the theory: confirm whether your suspected cause is correct before you commit to a fix. If not confirmed, form a new theory.

quiz.q: Why should you change only one thing at a time when testing?
options: So you know which change actually fixed or affected the issue
quiz.why: Changing one variable at a time means you can attribute the result to that change; changing several at once hides what actually worked.

quiz.q: What does 'verify full system functionality' mean?
options: Confirm the original issue is fixed and nothing else broke
quiz.why: After applying a fix you confirm the original symptom is gone and the rest of the system still works, ideally with the user, before closing.

quiz.q: List the six steps of the A+ troubleshooting methodology in order.
quiz.answer: 1) Identify the problem; 2) Establish a theory of probable cause; 3) Test the theory; 4) Establish a plan of action and implement the solution; 5) Verify full system functionality and apply preventive measures; 6) Document findings, actions, and outcomes.
quiz.why: Following the steps in order keeps troubleshooting systematic and repeatable rather than a guessing game.

quiz.q: Why is the final documentation step important even after the fix works?
quiz.answer: Documentation records what was wrong and how it was fixed so the same issue can be solved faster next time and feeds the knowledge base.
quiz.why: Good documentation turns one solved ticket into reusable knowledge for the whole team and prevents repeated investigation.

body_markdown:
## Why method beats guessing

Beginners often troubleshoot by trying random fixes until something works. It feels productive but it is slow, it breaks things, and you can never explain what fixed the issue. The **CompTIA A+ troubleshooting methodology** is a six-step model that turns troubleshooting into a repeatable, professional process. Learn it once and use it on everything from a frozen laptop to a network outage.

```text
1. Identify the problem
2. Establish a theory of probable cause
3. Test the theory
4. Establish a plan of action and implement the solution
5. Verify full functionality and apply preventive measures
6. Document findings, actions, and outcomes
```

## Step 1: Identify the problem

Before you touch anything, **gather information**. Ask the user what happened, what changed, and when it started. Note exact error messages. A useful question script:

```text
"When did this start?"
"What were you doing right before it happened?"
"Has anything changed recently - updates, new software, a move?"
"Does it happen every time, or sometimes?"
```

Also check the obvious: is it plugged in, is anyone else affected? Identifying scope early tells you whether this is one machine or an outage.

## Step 2: Establish a theory of probable cause

Form a **single, testable theory**. Start with the **most likely and simplest** cause — the famous principle is to question the obvious. "The password is wrong" or "the cable is loose" before "the motherboard has failed." Use your knowledge and the symptoms to make an educated guess, not a wild one.

## Step 3: Test the theory

Now **test it**. If your theory is right, you have found the cause. If it is wrong, form a *new* theory — do not start guessing randomly. Change **one thing at a time** so you always know what affected the result. If you cannot confirm a cause, this is often where you **escalate**.

## Step 4: Plan and implement the solution

With the cause confirmed, decide *how* to fix it, considering impact. Will the fix require a reboot, downtime, or a heads-up to others? Then implement it cleanly. For risky fixes, note a way back.

## Step 5: Verify functionality and prevent recurrence

Confirm the **original symptom is gone** and that **nothing else broke**. Do this *with the user* where possible — they decide whether it is truly fixed. Then think about **prevention**: should a setting change, or a knowledge article be written, so this does not happen again?

## Step 6: Document everything

Finally, **document** the symptoms, the cause, the actions you took, and the outcome in the ticket. This is not paperwork for its own sake — it is what lets the next technician (often future-you) solve the same issue in minutes, and it feeds the **knowledge base**.

## Your task

A user reports: "My laptop won't connect to Wi-Fi since this morning, but my phone connects to the same network fine." Write out how you would work this ticket through all six steps. For each step, write one or two lines: the questions you would ask, your first theory, how you would test it, a plausible fix, how you would verify, and a one-line documentation summary.

slides.narration: Welcome back. This lesson teaches you the single most valuable habit on a service desk: a methodical way to troubleshoot. We're using the CompTIA A plus six-step model, a process used across the industry. By the end you'll be able to attack any problem in a calm, repeatable order, instead of guessing randomly and hoping something sticks. This skill alone will set you apart as a beginner.

slides.narration: Here's the whole model on one slide. Step one, identify the problem. Step two, establish a theory of probable cause. Step three, test that theory. Step four, plan and implement the solution. Step five, verify full functionality and apply preventive measures. And step six, document your findings, actions, and outcomes. Memorise this order. It appears on the A plus exam, and far more importantly, it'll guide you through every real ticket you ever work.

Write down the exact error messages. And check the scope, because if others are affected too, you might be looking at an outage, not one broken machine. These few questions on screen will uncover most of what you need before you've changed a single setting.

slides.title: Steps 2 & 3: Theorise and test
bullets: Form one simple, testable theory.
Question the obvious first.
Test it; if wrong, form a new theory.
Change one thing at a time.
slides.narration: Steps two and three go together. First, establish a theory of probable cause. Form one single, testable theory, and start with the most likely and simplest cause. Question the obvious: a wrong password or a loose cable before a failed motherboard. Then test that theory. If it's right, you've found the cause. If it's wrong, form a new theory rather than guessing wildly. And always change one thing at a time, so you know exactly what affected the result.

slides.title: Step 4: Plan and implement
bullets: Decide how to fix, considering impact.
Will it need a reboot or downtime?
Warn others if the fix affects them.
For risky fixes, note a way back.
slides.narration: Step four is to plan and implement the solution. Now that you've confirmed the cause, think about how to fix it, and what the impact will be. Will the fix need a reboot, or cause downtime? Should you warn other people first? Then implement it cleanly. For anything risky, make a note of how you'd undo it. A moment of planning here prevents you from turning a small fix into a bigger incident.

slides.title: Step 5: Verify and prevent
bullets: Confirm the original symptom is gone.
Check nothing else broke.
Verify with the user where possible.
Consider how to prevent a repeat.
slides.narration: Step five is to verify full functionality and apply preventive measures. Confirm the original symptom is gone, and just as importantly, that nothing else broke in the process. Do this with the user where you can, because they're the one who decides it's truly fixed. Then think about prevention. Should a setting be changed, or a knowledge article written, so this never happens again? A fix that prevents the next ticket is worth two that don't.

slides.title: Step 6: Document
bullets: Record symptoms, cause, actions, outcome.
Not paperwork, it is reusable knowledge.
Lets the next tech solve it in minutes.

slides.narration: Finally, step six: document everything. Record the symptoms, the cause, the actions you took, and the outcome, right there in the ticket. This isn't paperwork for its own sake. It's what lets the next technician, who's very often future-you, solve the same issue in minutes instead of starting from scratch. Good documentation turns a single solved ticket into reusable knowledge for the whole team. Never skip it.
